column1: # Lesson ID | Applied scenario / concept intuition | Your turn question | Solution and reason

PS-001|A sample space is a model of the experiment. Choose the level of detail before counting: two distinguishable dice produce ordered pairs, not just sums.|Two fair coins and a fair die are tossed together. How many atomic outcomes are there? What is P(exactly one head and an even number)?|There are 2×2×6=24 equally likely outcomes. HT or TH gives 2 coin outcomes; 2,4,6 gives 3 die outcomes. Favourable count=6, so probability=6/24=1/4.

PS-002|Before multiplying, write one blank for each decision. Before adding, ask whether cases overlap; if they do, correct for double-counting.|How many 3-digit strings use distinct digits from 0–9 if the first digit cannot be zero?|First position: 9 choices (1–9). Second: 9 remaining digits (including zero if unused). Third: 8 remaining. Total=9×9×8=648; do not use 10×9×8 because a leading zero is prohibited.

PS-003|Ordered arrangements are different even if they contain the same elements: ABC, ACB and BAC correspond to three distinct ordered results.|How many ways can five different books be arranged on a shelf if two named books must stay adjacent?|Treat the named pair as one block: four objects arrange in 4! ways. Inside the block two books can swap in 2! ways. Answer=4!×2=48.

PS-004|Selection without order forms a set. Factorials count ordered arrangements first, so divide by the internal reordering count r!.|From 7 people, choose a 3-person team containing a particular person. How many?|Fix the particular person, then choose any 2 of the remaining 6. Number=C(6,2)=15. Do not multiply by 3! because team positions are unlabeled.

PS-005|Probability axioms rule out impossible answers. Any event and its complement exhaust the sample space without overlap.|For P(A)=0.65, what is P(A complement)? Can P(A union B)=1.15?|P(A complement)=1−0.65=0.35. A union probability of 1.15 is impossible because every event has probability at most one. Check numerical answers against [0,1].

PS-006|Independence means learning one event does not update the probability of the other. Disjointness means the two cannot happen together.|If P(A)=0.4 and P(B)=0.5 and A,B are independent, calculate P(A union B).|Independence gives P(A intersection B)=0.4×0.5=0.2; inclusion-exclusion gives union=0.4+0.5−0.2=0.7. They are not disjoint since intersection is positive.

PS-007|Conditioning replaces the full universe with the cases satisfying the condition. Every probability in the calculation uses the new denominator.|A fair die is rolled. Given the result is even, what is P(result greater than 3)?|Conditioning space is {2,4,6}; values above 3 are {4,6}. Answer=2/3, not 3/6. The restricted denominator is the main conceptual step.

PS-008|A partition divides cases into mutually exclusive, exhaustive branches. Weight each branch's conditional probability by the chance of entering it.|Factory A makes 60% of items with 2% defects; factory B makes 40% with 5% defects. Find overall defect rate.|P(defect)=0.6×0.02+0.4×0.05=0.032, or 3.2%. Adding 2%+5% ignores different production shares.

PS-009|Reverse conditionals carefully. A rare event often stays rare even when a test has excellent sensitivity.|A 1%-prevalence condition has 90% sensitivity and 5% false-positive rate. What fraction of positive tests are true positives?|Out of 10,000 people, about 100 have the condition, 90 of these test positive; 9,900 do not, of whom 495 test positive. Positive predictive value=90/(90+495)=2/13≈15.38%.

PS-010|A joint distribution answers questions about pairs together; summing or integrating out one variable creates the corresponding marginal.|Suppose P(X=0,Y=0)=0.1, P(0,1)=0.2, P(1,0)=0.3, P(1,1)=0.4. Find P(X=1).|Sum over possible Y values: P(X=1)=0.3+0.4=0.7. All four joint cells sum to one, which checks that the joint table is valid.

PS-011|The CDF accumulates probability to the left: F(x)=P(X≤x). For a discrete variable it has jumps; for a continuous variable it often changes smoothly.|A fair die represents X. What are F(3) and P(2<X≤5)?|F(3)=3/6=1/2. P(2<X≤5)=F(5)−F(2)=5/6−2/6=1/2. Endpoint handling matters for discrete random variables.

PS-012|Expectation is a weighted average of values, not necessarily one of the possible outcomes. Weights come from the PMF.|Let X=0 with probability 0.7 and X=10 with probability 0.3. Find E[X] and E[2X+1].|E[X]=0×0.7+10×0.3=3. By linearity E[2X+1]=2E[X]+1=7. Linearity does not require independence.

PS-013|Variance measures squared spread about the mean. Computing E[X²]−E[X]² is often faster than expanding all deviations.|A fair Bernoulli variable takes 1 with probability 0.4 and 0 otherwise. Find its variance.|E[X]=0.4 and E[X²]=0.4, so Var(X)=0.4−0.16=0.24. Equivalently p(1−p)=0.4×0.6=0.24.

PS-014|Mean reacts to extreme values, median tracks the middle of an ordered list, and mode captures the most common observation.|Find mean, median, and mode of 2,3,3,4,18. Which statistic better describes a typical value?|Mean=(2+3+3+4+18)/5=6; median=3; mode=3. The outlier 18 pulls up the mean, so the median better describes the central cluster.

PS-015|Conditioning changes both the expected value and spread by limiting the possibilities. The law of total variance separates within-group and between-group uncertainty.|A group has equal numbers of people from classes A and B with means 10 and 20. Find overall mean.|E[X]=E[E[X given class]]=0.5×10+0.5×20=15. You need class probabilities to average conditional expectations correctly.

PS-016|Positive covariance means variables tend to move together, negative means opposite movement; correlation removes units and bounds scale between −1 and 1.|If Y=−3X+7 and Var(X)=4, find Cov(X,Y) and Corr(X,Y).|Cov(X,Y)=Cov(X,−3X+7)=−3Var(X)=−12. Since Y is an exact decreasing affine function, Corr(X,Y)=−1 (for nonzero variance).

PS-017|Bernoulli is the one-trial success/failure building block. Its parameter p is the probability of 1, not necessarily the frequency in one sample.|A biased coin has P(head)=0.8. Let X indicate heads. Find E[X] and P(X=0).|X~Bernoulli(0.8), E[X]=0.8, P(X=0)=1−0.8=0.2. Repeating the trial independently gives a binomial count.

PS-018|The binomial counts successes across n independent identically distributed Bernoulli trials. Combinations count where successes may appear.|A fair coin is tossed 4 times. Find the probability of exactly 3 heads.|Choose which 3 of 4 positions contain heads: C(4,3)=4. Each length-4 sequence has probability (1/2)^4. Thus P(X=3)=4/16=1/4.

PS-019|For geometric trials the question is when the first success occurs, not how many successes appear. Uniform choices require truly equal probabilities.|A success occurs independently with probability 1/4 per attempt. Find P(first success on attempt 3).|Two failures then one success: (3/4)²×(1/4)=9/64. The geometric distribution is memoryless, not uniformly spread over trial numbers.

PS-020|A density is probability per unit of x; it can exceed one. Probability is area under a PDF over a specified interval.|Suppose f(x)=cx for 0≤x≤2 and zero otherwise. Find c.|Normalize total area: integral from 0 to 2 of cx dx = c[x²/2]_0²=2c=1. Hence c=1/2. A PDF itself is not P(X=x).

PS-021|Uniform continuous variables have constant height across an interval. Probabilities depend on length ratios, not numbers of integer points.|X is uniform on [2,12]. What is P(5≤X≤9)?|Interval length is 10; favourable interval length is 4. Probability=4/10=0.4. Exact endpoints carry zero probability for continuous distributions.

PS-022|Exponential waiting times are memoryless. The rate λ is events per time, so the mean wait is 1/λ.|Suppose service completion time is exponential with mean 4 minutes. Find P(wait more than 8 minutes).|λ=1/4 per minute. Survival P(X>8)=exp(−λ×8)=e^(−2)≈0.1353. Do not substitute the mean as λ.

PS-023|Poisson describes independent event counts within a fixed interval; exponential describes waiting between events in the corresponding process.|A web server receives 2 requests per minute on average. Under a Poisson model, find P(exactly 0 in one minute).|X~Poisson(2). P(X=0)=e^(−2)2^0/0!=e^(−2)≈0.1353. Here λ describes the expected count in the one-minute interval.

PS-024|Standardization converts a measurement into a dimensionless distance from the mean in standard deviations.|A variable is normal with mean 50 and standard deviation 10. Find P(X≤60) approximately.|z=(60−50)/10=1. Therefore P(X≤60)=P(Z≤1)≈0.8413 using a standard normal table or calculator.

PS-025|t accounts for estimating population spread with a sample, while chi-square often summarizes sums of squared standard-normal quantities.|A sample of n=9 from a normal population uses the sample standard deviation. What is the t degrees of freedom?|With one estimated mean, degrees of freedom=n−1=8. The test statistic (sample mean−claimed mean)/(s/√n) uses t_8 when population σ is unknown.

PS-026|Joint density describes a surface; integrate over the other coordinate to obtain a marginal and divide to condition.|Suppose f(x,y)=2 on the triangle 0<y<x<1 and zero otherwise. Find marginal f_X(x).|For fixed x in (0,1), integrate y from 0 to x: f_X(x)=∫0^x 2dy=2x. Check ∫0^1 2x dx=1.

PS-027|The LLN says averages stabilize; the CLT describes the approximate shape of normalized averages as sample size grows. These are different claims.|For i.i.d. variables with mean 20 and variance 25, estimate the standard deviation of the sample mean for n=100.|Var(sample mean)=25/100=0.25, so its standard deviation is 0.5. The CLT provides an approximate normal shape under suitable conditions.

PS-028|An estimate changes between samples. Standard error measures that sampling variability, whereas standard deviation measures spread of individual values.|A population has standard deviation 12. For a simple independent sample of 36, find the standard error of its mean.|SE=σ/√n=12/6=2. Increasing n by a factor of four halves the SE rather than reducing it fourfold.

PS-029|A 95% confidence method has 95% long-run coverage. It does not assign a 95% posterior probability to the fixed unknown parameter.|For known σ=10, n=100 and sample mean=50, construct approximate 95% z-interval.|SE=10/√100=1. Margin≈1.96×1=1.96. Interval≈[48.04,51.96]. The formula assumes an appropriate sampling model.

PS-030|A p-value is a probability of results at least as extreme under the null hypothesis, not the probability that the null is true.|A valid test gives p=0.03. Which significance levels reject H0: 1% or 5%?|Reject at α=0.05 because 0.03<0.05; do not reject at α=0.01 because 0.03>0.01. Failing to reject does not prove H0.

PS-031|Choose z or t based on what is known, sample size, and the statistical model; identify one-sided versus two-sided alternatives before computing a p-value.|A sample of n=25 has mean=12 and sample SD=5. Test mean=10 using a one-sample t statistic. Find t.|t=(12−10)/(5/√25)=2/(5/5)=2 with df=24. Whether this is significant depends on tail direction and α.

PS-032|Chi-square can test categorical independence via observed versus expected cell counts; do not confuse it with a t-test for numerical means.|In a 2×3 table of counts with fixed margins, how many degrees of freedom for independence?|df=(rows−1)(columns−1)=(2−1)(3−1)=2. Expected count in a cell=(row total×column total)/grand total.

LA-001|Vectors encode direction and magnitude. The dot product measures alignment and appears in projections, similarity and linear models.|Compute the dot product and Euclidean norm of x=(3,4) and y=(1,−2).|x·y=3×1+4×(−2)=−5. ||x||=√(3²+4²)=5. A negative dot product means an obtuse angle between nonzero vectors.

LA-002|A vector space permits addition and scalar multiplication without leaving the space. The zero vector must be included in every subspace.|Is the set S={(x,y): x+y=1} a subspace of R²?|No: (0,0) does not satisfy x+y=1. The set is an affine line, not a linear subspace. Compare with x+y=0, which is a subspace.

LA-003|A basis is a minimal independent spanning set. Dimension counts free directions, not the number of vectors you happen to list.|Do vectors (1,0), (0,1), (1,1) form a basis of R²? Why?|They span R² but are linearly dependent because (1,1)=(1,0)+(0,1). A basis of R² has exactly two independent vectors.

LA-004|Dependence means a nonzero coefficient combination gives zero; this is the algebraic signal of redundant information.|Are v1=(1,2), v2=(2,4) independent?|No. v2=2v1, so 2v1−v2=0 is a nontrivial relation. Dependence can be spotted visually as collinearity in R².

LA-005|Matrix multiplication composes linear transformations. The order often matters because AB generally differs from BA.|For A=[[1,2],[0,1]] and x=(3,4), calculate Ax.|Ax=(1×3+2×4,0×3+1×4)=(11,4). Think of A as a rule mapping the input vector to a transformed output.

LA-006|The determinant measures signed area or volume scaling. A zero determinant signals a collapsed direction and noninvertibility.|What is det([[2,4],[1,2]]) and what does its value say?|Determinant=2×2−4×1=0. Its columns are dependent, so it cannot be inverted and Ax=b need not have a unique solution.

LA-007|Rank counts independent columns; nullity counts free dimensions solving Ax=0. Rank-nullity adds up to the number of columns.|A 3×5 matrix has rank 3. What is its nullity?|Nullity=number of columns−rank=5−3=2. Thus its homogeneous system has a two-dimensional solution space.

LA-008|Row operations preserve solution sets, and reduced row echelon form exposes pivots and free variables.|Solve x+y=3 and x−y=1 by eliminating x or y.|Subtract second equation from first: 2y=2, so y=1 and x=2. Both equations should hold when substituted back.

LA-009|An augmented matrix tracks whether a linear system has no solution, one solution or infinitely many.|If row reduction yields [0 0 | 1], what does the system tell you?|It asserts 0=1, a contradiction. The system is inconsistent and has no solution regardless of the remaining rows.

LA-010|Eigenvectors preserve their direction under a transformation, while eigenvalues tell the amount and sign of stretching along them.|Find eigenvalues of diag(2,−3).|For a diagonal matrix, eigenvalues are diagonal entries: 2 and −3. Eigenvectors lie along the corresponding coordinate axes.

LA-011|Diagonalization A=PDP^−1 converts complicated repeated transformations to easy powers of diagonal entries.|For D=diag(2,3), compute D^4.|Raise each diagonal eigenvalue to the fourth power: D^4=diag(16,81). This is why diagonalizable matrices are useful for repeated updates.

LA-012|An orthogonal projection removes the component perpendicular to a subspace; the leftover residual is orthogonal to the projected space.|Project x=(3,4) onto the x-axis.|The projection is (3,0), because the x-axis keeps the first coordinate. Residual=(0,4), perpendicular to the x-axis.

LA-013|Idempotence means applying the same matrix twice has the same effect as once; projection matrices provide a geometric model.|If P=diag(1,0), compute P² and interpret it.|P²=diag(1,0)=P. Projecting onto the x-axis a second time changes nothing; this is idempotence.

LA-014|Quadratic forms xᵀAx classify curvature. Positive definiteness means strictly positive values for every nonzero vector.|Is A=diag(2,−1) positive definite?|No. With x=(0,1), xᵀAx=−1<0, while x=(1,0) gives 2>0. The form is indefinite.

LA-015|LU factors a matrix into elimination steps L and an upper triangular U; solving two triangular systems is efficient.|For A=[[2,1],[4,3]], show one elimination multiplier to remove 4 beneath pivot 2.|Multiplier=4/2=2. Subtract 2×row1 from row2 to obtain [0,1]. L records that multiplier, and U is upper triangular.

LA-016|SVD factors any matrix into orthogonal directions and nonnegative singular-value scales; small singular values identify near-lost directions.|For A=diag(3,1), what are its singular values?|They are 3 and 1, because singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of AᵀA=diag(9,1). Unlike eigenvalues, singular values are nonnegative.

LA-017|Least squares finds the best approximate solution when exact equality is impossible; its residual is orthogonal to column space.|Fit one constant c to observations 1,2,9 using least squares. What c minimizes squared error?|Minimize (1−c)²+(2−c)²+(9−c)². Derivative=6c−24=0, giving c=4, the sample mean.

CA-001|A function matches each input to one output. Domain restrictions determine where expressions and graph interpretations are meaningful.|Find the real domain of f(x)=1/(x−2) and g(x)=√(x+3).|For f, x≠2 because division by zero is undefined. For g, x≥−3 because the real square root requires nonnegative input.

CA-002|A limit is about what values approach, not necessarily the function value at the point itself.|Evaluate lim x→2 (x²−4)/(x−2).|Factor numerator=(x−2)(x+2). For x≠2 cancel and take limit x+2→4. Direct substitution at x=2 would give 0/0, not the answer.

CA-003|Continuity requires the two-sided limit to exist and equal f(c). A hole, jump or infinite behaviour breaks it.|Let f(x)=x+1 for x≠2, but f(2)=10. Is f continuous at 2?|No. Limit as x→2 is 3 but f(2)=10. Redefining f(2)=3 would fill the removable discontinuity.

CA-004|A derivative is local rate of change and tangent slope. Derivation from first principles helps catch formula memorization errors.|Differentiate f(x)=x³+2x using basic rules.|f′(x)=3x²+2. At x=1 the graph's tangent slope is 5. The derivative is itself a function of x.

CA-005|The mean value theorem connects a secant slope across an interval to at least one instantaneous slope inside it.|For f(x)=x² on [1,3], find c satisfying MVT.|Average slope=(9−1)/(3−1)=4. Since f′(c)=2c, set 2c=4 giving c=2, inside (1,3).

CA-006|Taylor series replaces a complicated function locally with a polynomial whose derivatives match at the centre.|Approximate e^0.1 using 1+x+x²/2.|1+0.1+0.01/2=1.105. Exact e^0.1≈1.10517, so the second-order Taylor approximation is close near zero.

CA-007|Stationary points f′=0 are only candidates. Look at the sign of the derivative on either side before calling them maxima or minima.|Find and classify the stationary point of f(x)=x²−4x+5.|f′=2x−4=0 at x=2. Derivative changes negative→positive across 2, so it is a local minimum with f(2)=1.

CA-008|The second derivative describes curvature near a stationary point; f″<0 indicates concave down locally.|Classify x=0 for f(x)=−x²+3.|f′(0)=0 and f″(0)=−2<0; therefore x=0 is a strict local maximum, with value 3.

CA-009|For global optima on a closed interval, check critical points and both endpoints rather than stopping at the first derivative root.|Find maximum of f(x)=x² on [−2,1].|Candidates are x=0 (stationary) and endpoints −2,1. Function values: 0,4,1. Maximum=4 at x=−2.

CA-010|Gradient descent moves opposite the derivative. Learning rate controls the step length, not just its direction.|For f(x)=(x−3)², x₀=0, and step size η=0.1, find the next iterate.|f′(x)=2(x−3), so f′(0)=−6. Update x₁=x₀−ηf′(0)=0−0.1(−6)=0.6, closer to the minimum at x=3.

PDSA-001|Python expressions follow operator precedence and type rules; a variable is a name bound to an object, not a fixed box with one type forever.|What are the outputs of -7//3, -7%3 and type(7/2) in Python 3?|Floor division is −3; modulo is 2 because −7=3×(−3)+2; true division gives 3.5 of type float. Flooring is not truncating toward zero.

PDSA-002|A loop repeats an operation over an iterable; think about start, stop and step before simulating code.|What does list(range(2,9,3)) produce?|It produces [2,5,8]. Start is inclusive, stop=9 is exclusive, step=3. Negative steps reverse traversal direction.

PDSA-003|A function evaluates local variables on each call; recursion must have a base case and progress toward it.|What is fact(4) if fact(n)=1 for n≤1 and otherwise n×fact(n−1)?|fact(4)=4×fact(3)=4×3×2×1=24. Each call reduces n by one until the base case is reached.

PDSA-004|Slices use half-open intervals [start:stop:step]. Lists mutate in place while tuples are immutable.|For a=[10,20,30,40,50], find a[1:4:2] and a[-1].|a[1:4:2]=[20,40], corresponding to indices 1 and 3. a[-1]=50. Index 4 is excluded from the slice stop.

PDSA-005|A dictionary maps hashable keys to values, whereas a set keeps only unique hashable members. Membership can be fast on average.|Evaluate len(set([1,1,2,3,3])) and {'a':2}.get('b',0).|Unique members are {1,2,3}, so length=3. The absent key uses the provided default, yielding 0 without KeyError.

PDSA-006|Asymptotic analysis compares growth as n becomes large. Ignore constant factors but not nested multiplication or exponential growth.|What is complexity of two nested loops each ranging over n items?|Each outer iteration does n inner operations, for n×n=n² in total, so Θ(n²). If loops are consecutive rather than nested, complexity is Θ(n).

PDSA-007|Space complexity tracks extra storage, not just runtime. Recursive calls consume stack frames even if the algorithm stores no explicit list.|A recursive function goes depth n using O(1) local memory per frame. What auxiliary space does it need?|O(n) call-stack space, because n frames coexist at the deepest point. Compare iterative loops often using O(1) auxiliary space.

PDSA-008|Arrays allow indexed access; linked lists favor pointer changes once the location is known. Complexity depends on the operation and representation.|What is worst-case time to access the kth node in a singly linked list?|O(k), which is O(n) in the worst case, because links must be followed sequentially. An array provides O(1) random index access.

PDSA-009|A stack is last-in-first-out; nesting, backtracking and expression parsing naturally use it.|Push 2, then 5, pop once, push 7. What is popped next?|After pop, 5 is removed; stack is [2]. Push 7 gives [2,7], so next pop yields 7.

PDSA-010|A queue is first-in-first-out, so it models arrivals and level-order traversal. A circular buffer reuses vacated slots.|Enqueue A, B, C, dequeue twice, enqueue D. What is at the front?|A and B leave first, leaving C and then D. The front is C, because queues remove the earliest remaining item.

PDSA-011|Trees organize parent-child relationships without cycles. Height, depth, leaves and branching factor describe different properties.|A rooted tree has root R with children A,B; A has child C. Which are leaves and what is depth of C?|Leaves are B and C, because neither has children. Depth(C)=2 edges from root R. Tree height is the maximum root-to-leaf depth.

PDSA-012|BST ordering makes search efficient when balanced, but a skewed tree behaves like a linked list.|Insert 5,2,8,1 into an empty BST. Which node is left child of 2?|1 is left child of 2 because 1<2<5. Searching a balanced BST is O(log n) but worst case O(n) when unbalanced.

PDSA-013|Traversal order encodes how a recursive algorithm handles parent and children. Inorder of a BST produces ascending keys.|For root 2 with left child 1 and right child 3, what are preorder and inorder?|Preorder root-left-right gives 2,1,3; inorder left-root-right gives 1,2,3. Reciting the visit rule is safer than memorizing outputs.

PDSA-014|Binary search halves a sorted search interval; without sorted data its comparisons have no justified direction.|Sorted list [1,4,7,9,12] is searched for 9. What first midpoint value is compared?|Middle index floor((0+4)/2)=2, value 7; since 9>7 search right half [9,12]. Overall time is O(log n).

PDSA-015|Elementary sorts reveal comparison versus movement costs. Selection sort does few swaps; insertion sort adapts to nearly sorted data.|What is worst-case time complexity of insertion sort and its best-case complexity?|Worst case Θ(n²) when each item must shift across many earlier items; best case Θ(n) when input is already sorted and only one comparison per insertion is needed.

PDSA-016|Merge sort divides input and merges sorted halves. Its recurrence adds linear merge work at each level.|Solve T(n)=2T(n/2)+n for power-of-two n.|There are log₂n recursion levels; total merge work per level is n. Thus T(n)=Θ(n log n), with typical O(n) extra array storage.

PDSA-017|Quicksort partitions around a pivot; balance of partitions controls complexity.|What recurrence describes a worst-case quicksort partition where pivot is always smallest?|T(n)=T(n−1)+Θ(n), summing to Θ(n²). Balanced partitions give average/typical Θ(n log n), but not guaranteed worst-case.

PDSA-018|Graphs represent relationships between vertices. Directed edges have orientation; undirected edges can be traversed both ways.|An undirected simple graph has 4 vertices all connected to each other. How many edges?|Complete graph K4 has 4×3/2=6 edges. Divide by 2 because every unordered pair is counted twice by 4×3.

PDSA-019|BFS uses a queue and explores hop distance; DFS uses a stack or recursion and follows depth first.|In an unweighted graph, which traversal finds a shortest path in number of edges, BFS or DFS?|BFS: it visits vertices in nondecreasing hop distance from the source. DFS may follow a long branch before noticing a shorter path.

PDSA-020|Dijkstra repeatedly finalizes the smallest tentative distance; it relies on nonnegative edge weights.|There are edges A→B weight 3, A→C weight 10, B→C weight 2. Find shortest A→C cost.|Compare direct route cost 10 with A→B→C cost 3+2=5. Shortest cost=5. Negative edges would invalidate standard Dijkstra assumptions.

PDSA-021|A topological ordering exists exactly for directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Each directed edge points forward in the order.|For edges A→C, B→C, C→D, give one valid topological order.|A,B,C,D is valid; B,A,C,D is also valid. No node can precede a prerequisite pointing into it. Cycles prevent such an ordering.

DB-001|ER diagrams describe entities and relationships before table implementation. Multiplicities determine where foreign keys usually belong.|Students enroll in many courses; each course has many students. What schema pattern fits?|Create Student(student_id), Course(course_id), and Enrollment(student_id,course_id) as a junction table. Many-to-many relationships cannot be represented by one foreign key without duplication.

DB-002|Keys uniquely identify rows. Candidate keys are minimal; a primary key is one chosen candidate key; foreign keys reference other rows.|A table has columns student_id, email and name, and both ID and email are guaranteed unique. How many candidate keys are obvious?|Two: {student_id} and {email}, assuming each is individually minimal and non-null. Either can be chosen as the primary key.

DB-003|Relational algebra selection filters rows (σ); projection keeps columns (π). SQL SELECT and WHERE reverse these names in everyday speech.|For Employees(name,salary), write algebra for names of people paid >50000.|π_name(σ_salary>50000(Employees)). First filter qualifying tuples; then retain only the name attribute.

DB-004|Joins combine matching rows across tables; Cartesian product without a join predicate usually creates far too many combinations.|A has 3 rows and B has 4 rows. How many rows does their Cartesian product contain?|3×4=12 rows, because every A row pairs with every B row. An equijoin may return fewer or more than the smaller table depending on repeated matching keys.

DB-005|Tuple relational calculus describes what rows satisfy a logical predicate rather than how to compute them.|Informally express “names of employees with salary above 50,000” in tuple calculus.|{t.name : t∈Employees and t.salary>50000}. The statement identifies qualifying tuples; SQL or relational algebra expresses a computation strategy.

DB-006|SQL WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; careful NULL handling is essential because SQL uses three-valued logic.|Write SQL to get names from Employee for salaries over 50000, sorted highest salary first.|SELECT name FROM Employee WHERE salary > 50000 ORDER BY salary DESC; The ORDER BY column need not be in the SELECT list in typical SQL queries.

DB-007|GROUP BY forms categories; aggregate functions summarize rows per group; HAVING filters group summaries after aggregation.|Write SQL to list department IDs having more than 5 employees.|SELECT dept_id FROM Employee GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5; A WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 clause is invalid because WHERE runs before aggregation.

DB-008|INNER JOIN keeps matches; LEFT JOIN also keeps unmatched left rows, using NULL for missing right-side values.|Which join shows all students even if no enrollment is found?|Student LEFT JOIN Enrollment ON Student.id=Enrollment.student_id. An INNER JOIN would omit students with no enrollment rows.

DB-009|EXISTS tests whether at least one matching row exists; NOT EXISTS is useful for set difference and universal quantification patterns.|Find customers with no orders. Which SQL pattern avoids NULL-related NOT IN traps?|SELECT c.id FROM Customer c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id); It tests nonexistence directly.

DB-010|Functional dependency X→Y says X determines Y. It is a statement about all valid rows, not a coincidence in one dataset.|If student_id→student_name, can one student_id have two distinct names in a valid instance?|No. A functional dependency requires any two rows with the same student_id to have the same student_name, for all valid instances.

DB-011|Normalization reduces update, insertion and deletion anomalies by separating independent facts into suitable relations.|Why is a table (student_id, student_name, course_id, course_name) potentially problematic?|Course name repeats for every enrolled student. Updating one course name requires many row changes. Separate Student, Course and Enrollment relations to avoid this update anomaly.

DB-012|Files can store records in heap, sorted or hashed order; the layout affects scans, equality lookups and range queries.|Which organization best supports efficient range scans on a frequently filtered ordered key: heap or sorted file?|Sorted organization, because matching records can be located and read in key order; heaps may require scanning many unrelated rows.

DB-013|A B+ tree stores searchable keys in internal nodes and data references in leaves; linked leaves help range scans.|Why would a B+ tree index often outperform a hash index for BETWEEN 100 AND 200?|The B+ tree keeps keys ordered and can scan adjacent leaves; hashing scatters nearby numeric keys and is best suited to exact key equality queries.

DB-014|ACID provides atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. A transaction succeeds as a logical whole or is rolled back.|A bank transfer debits one account but fails before crediting the other. Which ACID property should prevent partial success?|Atomicity: either both updates commit, or neither does. Consistency then preserves constraints such as total balance, assuming correct business logic.

DB-015|Data types and missing values influence model calculations. Missing does not mean zero unless zero is a meaningful observation.|A column “age” contains NULL for unknown ages. Why should you not replace every NULL with 0?|It would invent newborn ages and distort means and model signals. Choose an imputation strategy based on missingness and the task.

DB-016|Standardization moves features to mean zero and unit variance; min-max scaling maps endpoints to a chosen interval.|For feature values 10,20,30, what is the min-max scaled value of 20 in [0,1]?|Apply (x−min)/(max−min)=(20−10)/(30−10)=0.5. Never fit scaler parameters on test data when evaluating a model.

DB-017|Discretization turns continuous numbers into bins; sampling selects observations. Both can lose information or introduce bias.|Using equal-width bins 0–10, 10–20 and 20–30, in which bin would 17 fall?|It belongs in the 10–20 bin. Define endpoint conventions (for example [10,20)) to avoid double counting values on boundaries.

DB-018|Compression saves storage, while feature representations encode useful structure. Lossless and lossy transformations have different guarantees.|Why might replacing all rare categories with “Other” reduce storage but lose information?|It compresses the representation by merging categories; after merging, the original rare label cannot be recovered. This is lossy encoding.

DB-019|A star schema has a central fact table with metrics and foreign keys to denormalized dimensions; snowflake normalizes dimensions.|A sales warehouse stores sales_amount and keys for date, store and product. Which table holds the numeric sales measure?|The fact table Sales(date_key,store_key,product_key,sales_amount). Dimensions describe entities for slicing and grouping.

DB-020|OLAP roll-up aggregates to a coarser level; drill-down reveals finer groups. These are different from filtering to one member.|Aggregating sales from city to state is roll-up or drill-down?|Roll-up: city totals are combined into broader state totals. Drilling down would move from state to cities or stores.

DB-021|Measures may be additive, semi-additive or nonadditive depending on dimensions. Ratios usually require recomputation from base totals.|Why must you not simply add two stores' average selling prices?|An average is nonadditive; compute (total revenue across both stores)/(total units across both). Adding averages ignores transaction counts.

ML-001|Supervised learning uses labelled targets; unsupervised learning searches patterns without target labels. Data splitting estimates generalization.|You have 1000 labelled rows. Why keep an untouched test set until the end?|Repeated model selection on the test set leaks information about test performance into the model choice, creating optimistic estimates. Use training and validation for development.

ML-002|A loss quantifies predictive error, whereas the training objective can also include penalties such as regularization.|For predictions [2,4] and truths [3,1], calculate mean squared error.|Errors are −1 and +3; squares 1 and 9; MSE=(1+9)/2=5. Squaring makes large errors count more heavily.

ML-003|Simple linear regression fits intercept and slope by minimizing squared residuals. Slope quantifies the expected change in prediction per unit x.|For a fitted line ŷ=2+3x, predict y when x=4 and interpret slope.|Prediction=2+3×4=14. The slope says every +1 in x increases the prediction by 3, assuming the model relation is appropriate.

ML-004|With many features, matrix notation compresses a family of linear equations. The intercept typically uses an all-ones column.|If X is n×p and w is p×1, what shape is yhat=Xw?|n×1, one predicted target for each of the n observations. Ensure intercept handling matches the design matrix.

ML-005|Ridge regression adds an L2 penalty to discourage very large coefficients; scaling matters when features have different units.|What happens qualitatively when ridge parameter λ increases greatly?|Coefficients shrink toward zero (often the unpenalized intercept excepted). Excessive λ can underfit. Ridge usually shrinks but does not set coefficients exactly to zero.

ML-006|Gradient descent iteratively updates parameters using derivative information; learning rate and scaling control convergence.|If loss gradient at w=5 is +4 and η=0.25, what is the new w?|w_new=w−η∇L=5−0.25×4=4. The step heads opposite the positive gradient.

ML-007|Logistic regression models class probability with sigmoid, not unbounded numerical outcomes. The decision threshold is a separate choice.|For logit z=0, what probability does sigmoid output?|σ(0)=1/(1+e^0)=1/2. A threshold of 0.5 classifies as positive when z≥0 under the usual convention.

ML-008|Precision asks how many predicted positives were correct; recall asks how many actual positives were found.|A classifier has TP=30, FP=10, FN=20, TN=40. Find precision and recall.|Precision=30/(30+10)=0.75; recall=30/(30+20)=0.60. Accuracy=(30+40)/100=0.70, which tells a different story.

ML-009|kNN stores training examples and predicts from nearby points. Feature scale and distance metric strongly affect the neighbor set.|With k=3 nearest neighbor labels [A,A,B], what class is predicted?|Majority voting predicts A. For regression, kNN usually averages neighbors' numerical targets instead.

ML-010|Naive Bayes applies Bayes' rule and assumes features independent conditioned on the class; its useful simplicity can work despite approximate assumptions.|If P(C)=0.4, P(x1|C)=0.5, P(x2|C)=0.3, what is the unnormalized posterior score under naive Bayes?|Score=P(C)P(x1|C)P(x2|C)=0.4×0.5×0.3=0.06. Normalize against competing-class scores to get actual posterior probability.

ML-011|LDA seeks discriminative directions using class means and shared covariance assumptions. It is not the same objective as PCA.|What simplifying covariance assumption distinguishes standard LDA classification?|Class-conditional feature distributions are modeled with a common covariance matrix. Differences between class means then determine linear decision boundaries.

ML-012|SVM maximizes a margin between classes while respecting or penalizing violations. Support vectors are the closest influential examples.|For hyperplane w·x+b=0, what is geometric margin expression for a correctly classified point (x,y∈±1)?|Signed distance=y(w·x+b)/||w||. Larger positive values mean more separation from the boundary.

ML-013|Decision trees repeatedly split data to reduce impurity, creating human-readable if-then paths. Deep trees can overfit.|A node has 50% class A and 50% class B. What is its Gini impurity?|Gini=1−(0.5²+0.5²)=0.5. A pure leaf with all one class has impurity zero.

ML-014|High bias misses structure, while high variance changes strongly with training samples. Model complexity can shift the balance.|A deep decision tree fits training data perfectly but performs poorly on unseen data. Which failure is likely?|High variance/overfitting. Use pruning, more data, feature controls or cross-validation before assuming the training fit is good generalization.

ML-015|Cross-validation rotates the validation portion to reuse limited data for model selection without contaminating the final test set.|For 200 examples, how many are validated in each 5-fold CV round?|200/5=40 held-out validation examples per fold; the other 160 train. Each example is in validation once over five rounds.

ML-016|A neuron transforms a weighted sum by an activation. Without nonlinear activations, multiple linear layers collapse to one linear map.|For inputs x=(2,3), weights w=(1,−2), bias b=4, what is a ReLU neuron's output?|Weighted sum z=1×2+(−2)×3+4=0; ReLU(0)=max(0,0)=0.

ML-017|An MLP chains linear transformations and nonlinear activations to represent complex decision surfaces. Track shapes layer by layer.|A network maps 4 inputs to 5 hidden units to 2 outputs. How many weight parameters excluding biases?|First layer 4×5=20; second 5×2=10; total 30. Bias parameters would add 5+2=7.

ML-018|Backpropagation applies the chain rule backward through layers to compute all parameter derivatives efficiently.|If y=(2x+1)², calculate dy/dx at x=2 using the chain rule.|Let u=2x+1. dy/du=2u, du/dx=2, so dy/dx=4(2x+1)=20 at x=2.

ML-019|Clustering groups similar observations without target labels. Results depend on similarity definition and geometry of data.|Would Euclidean k-means be sensitive if one feature is in meters and another in millimeters?|Yes. A large numerical scale dominates Euclidean distance; appropriate scaling may be needed before clustering.

ML-020|k-means alternates assignment to the nearest centroid and recomputation of means. Initialization affects the solution.|Given cluster points 1,3,8 on a line, what is their k-means centroid?|Mean=(1+3+8)/3=4. The centroid need not equal any observed point.

ML-021|k-medoids chooses a real data point as cluster representative and can be more robust to certain outliers.|For data points 1,2,20, which point minimizes total absolute distance to the others?|2: total |2−1|+|2−20|=19; point 1 totals 20, point 20 totals 37. A medoid is an existing observation.

ML-022|Hierarchical clustering builds a merge tree or splits an existing group. Dendrogram cut height controls cluster granularity.|Does agglomerative hierarchical clustering begin with one cluster or one cluster per observation?|One cluster per observation, then merges nearest clusters until one remains or a stop rule is met. Divisive clustering proceeds the other way.

ML-023|Linkage defines distance between two clusters: single uses the closest pair; complete uses the farthest pair.|Cluster A={0,2}, B={6,9} on a line. Find single- and complete-link distances.|Single link=min pair distance=|2−6|=4; complete link=max pair distance=|0−9|=9. Different linkage rules produce different dendrograms.

ML-024|PCA rotates coordinates toward directions of maximum variance without using class labels. Center data before covariance decomposition.|If covariance matrix is diag(9,1), what fraction of variance does the first principal component explain?|Largest eigenvalue=9; total variance=9+1=10; explained variance ratio=9/10=90%.

ML-025|Dimensionality reduction trades feature count against retained information and interpretability. Distinguish supervised and unsupervised objectives.|A PCA model retains eigenvalues 5,3 of a dataset with total variance 10. What variance fraction is retained?|Retained fraction=(5+3)/10=0.8 or 80%. This says nothing by itself about downstream classification accuracy.

AI-001|An AI search problem needs states, actions, transition model, starting state, goal test and costs. Poor formulation can create enormous search spaces.|For solving a maze, give example of state and action definitions.|A state can be the current cell (r,c). Actions are valid moves up/down/left/right, constrained by walls. Goal test checks reaching the destination.

AI-002|Uninformed search uses no goal-specific estimate; BFS and DFS differ in frontier order and completeness behaviour.|For a branching factor b and shallowest goal depth d, which algorithm generally finds shallowest unweighted solution?|BFS explores all depth-0, depth-1, ... nodes and finds a shallowest goal. It can use exponential memory O(b^d).

AI-003|Uniform-cost search prioritizes accumulated path cost g(n), not number of edges. It generalizes BFS to varying nonnegative costs.|A→B costs 1, B→G costs 10, A→G costs 5. Which solution does uniform-cost search prefer?|Direct A→G with total cost 5 rather than the two-edge route costing 11. It minimizes cost, not steps.

AI-004|A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining distance to a goal; useful estimates guide exploration. Admissibility means never overestimating true remaining cost.|True remaining cost is 7. Can h(n)=9 be admissible for that state?|No. It overestimates 7 by 2. An admissible heuristic must satisfy h(n)≤h*(n) at every relevant state.

AI-005|A* evaluates f(n)=g(n)+h(n). With a suitable consistent heuristic, graph search finds optimal routes without repeatedly reopening settled nodes.|Node X has g=4,h=3; node Y has g=6,h=0. Which has lower A* priority?|X has f=7; Y has f=6, so Y is chosen first from the open set. Lower f is preferred, not necessarily lower g.

AI-006|Minimax alternates maximizing and minimizing decisions in adversarial games. It assumes rational play by the opponent.|A MAX root has two MIN children, whose leaf payoffs are [3,8] and [5,6]. Which branch does MAX choose?|Left MIN returns min(3,8)=3; right MIN returns min(5,6)=5. MAX chooses right, guaranteeing value 5 against optimal opposition.

AI-007|Alpha-beta pruning discards branches that cannot affect minimax decisions, without changing the result if implemented correctly.|In MAX/MIN search, what does alpha represent?|Alpha is the best value MAX can guarantee along the path so far; beta is the best bound MIN can enforce. When alpha≥beta, remaining descendants can be pruned.

AI-008|Propositional logic assigns each statement true or false. Implication p→q is false only when p is true and q false.|Evaluate p→q when p=false, q=false.|True. Material implication is logically equivalent to (not p) OR q. It should not be confused with causal implication.

AI-009|Logical equivalences transform expressions without changing truth value; De Morgan laws distribute negation across AND/OR.|Negate “A AND B” in equivalent form.|NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B). For a negated universal condition, switch AND/OR or quantifiers carefully.

AI-010|First-order logic quantifies objects and describes relationships. The order of quantifiers changes meaning.|Are ∀x∃y Loves(x,y) and ∃y∀x Loves(x,y) equivalent?|No. The first says everyone loves someone (possibly different people); the second says there is one person loved by everyone.

AI-011|A knowledge base entails a statement when every model satisfying the KB also satisfies that statement. Syntax and semantics are different.|If KB contains P and P→Q, does KB entail Q?|Yes by modus ponens: every assignment satisfying both P and P→Q must make Q true. This is valid inference, not merely an observed correlation.

AI-012|A Bayesian network factorizes joint probabilities through directed parent relationships and conditional probability tables.|For network A→B→C, write the joint factorization.|P(A,B,C)=P(A)P(B|A)P(C|B). The graph makes conditional structure explicit and can reduce storage.

AI-013|d-separation reads conditional independence from active versus blocked trails in a DAG. Conditioning on a collider can open a path.|For chain A→B→C, are A and C independent given B under graph Markov assumptions?|Yes. Conditioning on B blocks the chain path. Without conditioning, dependence can travel through B.

AI-014|Variable elimination sums out hidden variables from the factorized joint distribution, combining only relevant factors along the way.|If P(A,B)=P(A)P(B|A), how do you compute P(B)?|Sum over A: P(B)=Σ_a P(a)P(B|a). In larger networks, elimination order affects intermediate factor size.

AI-015|Sampling approximates probabilities using generated observations. More effective samples generally reduce Monte Carlo variability.|Out of 1000 independent simulated draws, event E occurs 230 times. Estimate P(E).|Estimated probability=230/1000=0.23. The Monte Carlo standard error is approximately √[0.23×0.77/1000]≈0.0133.

GA-001|Grammar choices should preserve subject-verb agreement and consistent time. Focus on identifying the true subject of a long phrase.|Choose “The list of items is ready” or “The list of items are ready.”|“The list of items is ready” is correct because the grammatical subject is singular “list,” not plural “items.”

GA-002|Articles and prepositions depend on meaning and sound. “An” is based on the initial sound, not simply the first written letter.|Fill: “She is ___ honest engineer.”|“An honest engineer,” because honest starts with a vowel sound (the h is silent). “An” follows pronunciation, not spelling alone.

GA-003|Use surrounding sentence logic to infer vocabulary rather than guessing from a word's familiar appearance.|In “The evidence was scant,” is scant closer to “limited” or “abundant”?|Limited. “Scant” means barely sufficient or small in amount. Opposites in options often make contextual elimination efficient.

GA-004|Comprehension questions test what follows from the passage, not what feels plausible from outside knowledge.|A passage says “Some models improve with more data.” Can you infer “All models improve with more data”?|No. “Some” does not imply “all.” The stronger universal claim is not supported by the given sentence.

GA-005|Sequencing requires links between introductions, pronouns, cause and effect, and chronology. Track which sentence introduces each referent.|Arrange: A “It finally arrived.” B “Riya ordered a book.” C “She opened the package.”|B→A→C is natural: B introduces the book, A refers to its arrival, C describes the next action. Other contexts could alter sequence but not without cues.

GA-006|Percentage changes are multiplicative. Sequential +20% and −20% do not cancel unless based on the same original amount.|A price rises 20%, then falls 20%. What is net percentage change?|100→120→96, so it falls 4% overall. Multipliers 1.2×0.8=0.96 are safer than adding signed percentages.

GA-007|Weighted averages use group sizes as weights; simple averages apply only when every group has equal weight.|Class A has 20 students averaging 60; B has 30 averaging 80. Overall mean?|Combined total=20×60+30×80=3600; count=50; weighted mean=3600/50=72.

GA-008|Exponent rules follow multiplication of equal bases; logs invert exponentiation. Note domains of real logarithms.|Solve log₂x=5.|x=2^5=32, since log₂32=5. For real logarithms, the argument x must be positive.

GA-009|Identify whether differences, ratios or alternating patterns are more regular than raw numbers.|Find next in 2,6,12,20,30,...|Differences are 4,6,8,10, so next difference 12 gives 42. Another view: terms n(n+1) for n=1,2,3,...

GA-010|Count ordered arrangements versus unordered selections separately and check whether repeated choices are allowed.|How many 2-digit PINs from 0–9 are possible if repetition is allowed and leading zero is allowed?|There are 10 choices for each slot, so 10×10=100. It is not a 2-digit integer restriction; “PIN” allows 00.

GA-011|Data-interpretation questions often hide unit conversion or different denominators. Read labels and axes before arithmetic.|A chart shows sales 200 in 2025 and 260 in 2026. Find percentage increase.|Increase=60; percentage increase=60/200×100=30%. The denominator for growth is the old value.

GA-012|Geometry becomes easier by decomposing shapes and using consistent units. Areas scale with length squared, volumes with length cubed.|A square's side doubles. By what factor does its area increase?|Area s² becomes (2s)²=4s²: factor 4. If a cube's side doubled its volume would grow by factor 8.

GA-013|Basic aptitude probability uses the same core ideas as statistics. List elementary possibilities rather than assuming symmetry from the labels.|A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. One is chosen uniformly. What is probability blue?|2 favourable blue balls out of 5 equally likely individual balls, so P(blue)=2/5.

GA-014|Deductive arguments guarantee conclusions under their premises; inductive arguments infer likely generalizations from samples.|Premises: All cats are mammals; Leo is a cat. What follows deductively?|Leo is a mammal. This is guaranteed by the premises, not just suggested by past observation.

GA-015|Reasoning puzzles benefit from explicit constraint tables, elimination and testing rather than memorized tricks.|Three people A,B,C stand in a line. A is to left of B; C is to right of B. What order must hold?|A B C, because A<B<C. Draw a three-slot diagram to avoid reversing the left/right restrictions.

GA-016|For rotations, track orientation and a landmark corner. Mirroring reverses handedness rather than merely turning the shape.|A clock hand initially points up. After clockwise quarter-turn, where does it point?|Right. A clockwise 90° rotation maps upward direction to rightward direction in the image plane.

GA-017|Paper-folding problems are symmetry problems in disguise. Reflect cut locations across each fold line to unfold.|A square paper is folded once exactly in half and one small hole is punched away from the fold. How many holes appear after opening?|Two holes, mirror images across the fold. A punch directly on the fold could produce a different count, so location matters.
